title: AQA GCSE Physics · Braking, Momentum and Work

items.stem: A driver sees a hazard, reacts, brakes, and brings the car safely to rest. Which distance is the stopping distance of the car?

options.text: The thinking distance added to the braking distance travelled
The distance travelled after the brake pedal is pressed
Only the distance travelled while the brakes act
The distance covered during the driver's reaction time

items.why: The specification defines stopping distance as the sum of the distance travelled during the driver's reaction time and the distance travelled under the braking force.

items.stem: What does the specification say about human reaction times?

options.text: They are the same for every driver, typically 0.7 s
They range from about 2 s to about 3 s for almost everyone
They vary from person to person, typically 0.2 s to 0.9 s
Every driver shares one fixed reaction time

items.why: The specification states that reaction times vary from person to person and that typical values range from 0.2 s to 0.9 s.

items.stem: Which pair of causes does the specification give for a longer braking distance?

options.text: A worn-out engine and an ageing gearbox in the car
Wet or icy roads, and worn brakes or worn tyres
Fog and darkness, which hide the hazard ahead
Driver tiredness and having drunk alcohol

items.why: Adverse road conditions are given as wet or icy conditions, and poor condition of the vehicle is limited to the vehicle's brakes or tyres.

items.stem: Two identical lorries brake with the same braking force, one from 15 m/s and one from 25 m/s. Which statement about their stopping distances is correct?

options.text: The 25 m/s lorry needs distance in proportion to speed
The lorry at 15 m/s needs a greater distance in which to stop
The lorry at 25 m/s needs the greater stopping distance
Its braking distance is just under twice as long

items.why: For a given braking force, the greater the speed of the vehicle the greater the stopping distance. The faster lorry travels further while the driver reacts, and further again under braking.

items.stem: Five students measure their own reaction times and obtain 0.21 s, 0.34 s, 0.28 s, 0.52 s and 0.45 s. What is the best conclusion to draw?

options.text: Four of the results must be wrong, as only one can be right
Everyone's reaction time is 0.36 s, the mean of the five
The results are unusable because they do not agree
Reaction times differ between people, as expected

items.why: Every value lies inside the typical range of 0.2 s to 0.9 s, and the spread between them is exactly what the specification means by reaction times varying from person to person.

items.stem: Which list contains only factors that the specification links to a driver's reaction time or ability to react?

options.text: Tiredness, alcohol, drugs, and distractions such as a phone
Tiredness, alcohol, icy roads and worn brake pads
Alcohol, drugs, heavy rain and under-inflated tyres
The driver's age, natural reflexes and their IQ

items.why: The specification names tiredness, drugs and alcohol as affecting reaction time, and adds that distractions may also affect a driver's ability to react.

items.stem: A driver holds a long hands-free phone conversation while driving. What does the specification say about this?

options.text: It has no effect, as the driver's hands stay on the wheel
Distractions may also affect a driver's ability to react
It lengthens the braking distance, not the thinking one
It matters only if the driver is also tired or drunk

items.why: The specification states that distractions may also affect a driver's ability to react. A slower reaction means a longer thinking distance and so a longer stopping distance.

items.stem: In the ruler drop test one student holds a ruler above a partner's open hand, releases it without warning, and the partner catches it as quickly as they can. Which measurement is taken, and what is done with it?

options.text: The time in seconds is read directly from the ruler scale
The number of centimetres is used as the time in seconds
The drop distance is measured, then converted to a time
The mass of the ruler is used to find the time of fall

items.why: The distance the ruler falls before it is caught is measured, then converted into a reaction time using a conversion chart or s = 1/2 g t2. A shorter drop means a shorter reaction time.

items.stem: A car is driven on an icy road at the same speed as it was on a dry road. Why is its braking distance longer on the ice?

options.text: The ice makes the vehicle heavier, so it takes far longer
The brakes themselves stop working when the road is icy
There is less grip, so a smaller braking force can act
The driver's reaction time is longer on an icy road

items.why: Ice reduces the friction available where the tyres meet the road, so the largest braking force that can be applied before the wheels lock is smaller and more distance is needed.

items.stem: A car has badly worn tyres. Which part of the stopping distance is increased, and why?

options.text: The thinking distance, because the driver is more cautious
The thinking distance, because tyres are part of the car
Neither, provided the driver brakes gently and early
The braking distance: the tyres grip the road less

items.why: Worn tread cannot clear water or bite into the road surface, so the friction force available for braking is smaller and the car travels further under braking.

items.stem: A force is applied to the brakes of a moving car. Which statement describes what happens to the energy?

options.text: Kinetic energy is destroyed by the friction in the brake pads
Kinetic energy is stored in the brakes ready for later reuse
Friction does work, heating the brakes and slowing the car
The kinetic energy simply disappears when the car stops

items.why: Work done by the friction force between the brakes and the wheel reduces the kinetic energy of the vehicle, and the temperature of the brakes increases.

items.stem: Two identical cars must each stop within the same distance, one from 12 m/s and the other from 24 m/s. Which needs the greater braking force, and why?

options.text: The car at 12 m/s, as a slow car is harder to stop
The car at 24 m/s needs less force, having more time
The 24 m/s car needs less force, with more road
The car at 24 m/s: more kinetic energy to remove

items.why: The greater the speed of a vehicle the greater the braking force needed to stop the vehicle in a certain distance. Four times as much kinetic energy must be removed over the same distance.

items.stem: A driver brakes very hard to avoid a collision, producing a very large deceleration. Why is this dangerous?

options.text: A very large braking force is needed, risking loss of control
A large deceleration always means a longer stopping distance
It is not dangerous, since stopping sooner is safer
The kinetic energy is destroyed at once, harming the car

items.why: The greater the braking force the greater the deceleration, and large decelerations may lead to the brakes overheating and to loss of control, for example if the wheels lock and the car skids.

items.stem: A lorry driver brakes heavily and repeatedly on a long, steep hill. What is the most likely consequence, and why?

options.text: The brakes cool down, as the lorry is slowing
The brakes overheat, so they become less effective
The kinetic energy of the lorry rises as it descends
The kinetic energy is stored in the brakes

items.why: Work done by the friction force raises the temperature of the brakes. Repeated heavy braking gives them no chance to cool, and overheated brakes lose their effectiveness.

items.stem: A car's speed doubles from 10 m/s to 20 m/s. The driver's reaction time and the braking force are unchanged. What happens to the two parts of the stopping distance?

options.text: Both the thinking distance and the braking distance double
Thinking distance doubles and braking distance quadruples
Thinking distance is unchanged, braking distance doubles
The stopping distance itself just doubles overall

items.why: Thinking distance = speed x reaction time, so it doubles. The kinetic energy is four times larger and the same braking force must remove it over a distance, so the braking distance becomes about four times larger.

items.stem: (Physics only) A car is driven at 13 m/s, a typical speed in a built-up area. The driver's reaction time is about 0.7 s, and the braking distance at this speed is about 14 m. Estimate the distance the car needs to make an emergency stop.

options.text: About 14 m, which is the braking distance
About 9 m, covered while the driver reacts
About 18 m: twice the thinking distance
About 23 m: 9 m thinking, 14 m braking

items.why: Thinking distance = 13 x 0.7, which is about 9 m. Adding the 14 m braking distance gives a stopping distance of about 23 m, the accepted value at 30 mph.

items.stem: On a dry road a car travelling at 31 m/s (about 70 mph) has a stopping distance of roughly 96 m, of which about 22 m is thinking distance. Estimate its stopping distance at the same speed on a wet road.

options.text: About 96 m, because the driver reacts just as quickly
About 170 m, since the braking part roughly doubles
About 48 m, as water lubricates the road well
About 31 m, one metre for each metre per second

items.why: The thinking distance of about 22 m is unchanged, but the braking distance of about 74 m roughly doubles on a wet surface, taking the total to somewhere near 170 m.

items.stem: (HT only) A car of mass 1200 kg travelling at 24 m/s brakes in an emergency and comes to rest in 3.0 s. Estimate the braking force acting on the car.

options.text: 28 800 N, from the mass times the car's velocity
3600 N, from mass x the 3.0 s stopping time
9600 N, from a = 8.0 m/s2 and then F = m a
150 N, from mass divided by deceleration

items.why: Deceleration a = change in velocity / time = 24 / 3.0 = 8.0 m/s2. Then F = m a = 1200 x 8.0 = 9600 N, a typical order of magnitude for emergency braking of a family car.

items.stem: (HT only) A van of mass 2000 kg slows from 18 m/s to 6 m/s in 4.0 s while braking on a public road. Estimate the braking force acting on the van.

options.text: 9000 N, taking the change as the full 18 m/s
36 000 N, from mass x the starting speed
500 N, which is a gentle everyday braking force
6000 N, from a deceleration of 3.0 m/s2

items.why: The velocity changes by 12 m/s in 4.0 s, so a = 12 / 4.0 = 3.0 m/s2. Then F = m a = 2000 x 3.0 = 6000 N, a plausible value for firm braking on a public road.

items.stem: (Physics only) A graph shows stopping distance on the vertical axis against speed on the horizontal axis for a family car. What shape is the line, and why?

options.text: A curve that gets steeper, as braking distance grows fastest
A straight line through the origin, as distance = speed
A straight line sloping steadily upward
A horizontal line, because the braking force is fixed

items.why: The thinking distance contribution is a straight line through the origin, but the braking distance contribution rises with speed squared, so the total curves upwards ever more steeply.

items.stem: (Physics only) Stopping distance is plotted against speed for a car and for a fully loaded lorry. At every speed shown the lorry's line lies above the car's line, and the gap between them widens as speed increases. What does the graph show?

options.text: The lorry driver has a longer reaction time than the car driver
The lorry needs a longer stopping distance at every speed
The lorry is always driven faster than the car is driven
Both lines are straight, so distance doubles with speed

items.why: Reading upwards from any speed on the horizontal axis gives a larger stopping distance for the lorry than for the car, and the difference between them grows as the speed increases.

items.stem: A student's five ruler drop results convert to 0.18 s, 0.20 s, 0.19 s, 0.65 s and 0.21 s. How should the student's reaction time be reported?

options.text: Average all five of the results to get about 0.29 s
Take the shortest result, 0.18 s, as the best attempt
Keep all readings, since none may be discarded
Discard 0.65 s and average the other four results

items.why: 0.65 s stands well clear of the tight cluster near 0.19 s and is almost certainly a lapse of attention rather than a genuine reaction. The mean of the remaining four is about 0.20 s.

items.stem: At 20 m/s a rested driver has a thinking distance of 14 m, from a reaction time of 0.7 s. When tired, the same driver at the same speed has a thinking distance of 18 m. What does the data show?

options.text: The tired driver's reaction time has risen to about 0.9 s
The reaction time has risen to about 2.5 s when tired
The reaction time is unchanged; the car was faster
The reaction time fell, as tiredness slows the car down

items.why: Thinking distance = speed x reaction time, so 18 m divided by 20 m/s gives 0.9 s. Tiredness has lengthened this driver's reaction time by about 0.2 s.

items.stem: Heavy rain begins during a motorway journey. Which action best reflects the physics of stopping distance, and why?

options.text: Slow down and leave a bigger gap, as braking needs more road
Keep the same gap, since the reaction time is unchanged
Brake as hard as possible each time, to stop sooner
Drive faster, to spend less time out in the rain

items.why: Wet conditions reduce grip and so lengthen the braking distance, while the thinking distance is unchanged. Driving more slowly and leaving a larger gap restores the safety margin.

items.stem: The specification defines momentum by an equation. Which word equation is that definition?

options.text: momentum = mass × acceleration
momentum = weight × velocity
momentum = mass × velocity
momentum = force × velocity

items.why: This is the defining word equation given in 4.5.7.1, and it is one of the equations students are required to recall.

items.stem: Which symbol equation for momentum does the specification give?

options.text: p = m × a
p = ½ m v²
p = m v²
p = m v

items.why: The symbol form printed in 4.5.7.1: p for momentum, m for mass, v for velocity.

items.stem: Which unit does the specification give for momentum, p?

options.text: kilograms metre per second, kg m/s
kilogram per metre second, kg/m s
newtons per second squared, N/s²
newton metres per second, N m/s

items.why: The unit printed in 4.5.7.1, and the one built by multiplying kg by m/s.

items.stem: In a closed system the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it. What is this called?

options.text: Newton's third law of motion
Conservation of net force
Conservation of momentum
Conservation of energy

items.why: This is the name the specification gives to the statement in 4.5.7.2.

items.stem: (physics only) Which two equations does the specification combine to give F = (m ∆v)/(∆t)?

options.text: F = m × a and a = (v - u)/(t)
p = m a and a = (v - u)/(t)
F = m × a and a = ∆v × ∆t
F = m × a and E = ½ m v²

items.why: These are the two equations named in 4.5.7.3; substituting the second into the first gives the momentum form.

items.stem: (physics only) In the equation F = (m ∆v)/(∆t), what does the quantity m ∆ v represent?

options.text: The force acting on the object, because force equals the change in momentum
The change in momentum, that is the mass multiplied by the change in velocity
The total momentum the object had before the force began to act on it, in kg m/s
The change in the force acting, which is the mass multiplied by the change in acceleration

items.why: The specification states directly that m ∆ v = change in momentum.

items.stem: A lorry's speed is given as 54 km/h. What must be done before this value is used in p = m v?

options.text: It must be converted to metres per second, by dividing by 3.6, because v in p = m v is in m/s
It can be put straight into p = m v as 54, because km/h is already a unit of speed
It can be substituted just as it is, provided the mass of the lorry is given in kilograms
It must be multiplied by 3.6, the number that converts between the two units of speed

items.why: The specification gives velocity, v, in metres per second, so a speed in km/h has to be converted first.

items.stem: Why is the unit of momentum kilograms metre per second?

options.text: Because it is the unit of force multiplied by the unit of the time for which that force acts
Because momentum is mass × acceleration, so the unit is kg multiplied by m/s² instead
Because momentum is a compound quantity, so its unit is always a compound unit too
Because momentum is mass × velocity, so the unit must be kg multiplied by m/s, or kg m/s

items.why: The unit of any quantity comes from the equation defining it: kg × m/s = kg m/s.

items.stem: The specification states conservation of momentum for a closed system. What is a closed system?

options.text: One in which the objects are all sealed inside a container, so that nothing can escape from it
One in which no mass enters or leaves and no resultant force acts on it from outside the system
One in which nothing is moving, so that the total momentum of the system stays equal to zero
One in which the objects touch each other, so that momentum can be passed from one to another

items.why: This is the condition under which the total momentum before an event equals the total momentum after it.

items.stem: Two skaters stand at rest on ice and push each other apart. Which statement about their momentum is correct?

options.text: They have equal and opposite momenta, so the total is still zero, as it was before the push
Both of the skaters are now moving, so the system has gained momentum from the push they gave
Each skater simply keeps the momentum it began with, which was zero for both
Their momenta add together, giving twice the momentum that one skater has on its own

items.why: The total momentum before the push is zero, and in a closed system the total after must also be zero.

items.stem: A moving trolley collides with a stationary trolley and slows down, while the second trolley moves off. Which description is correct?

options.text: Some momentum was destroyed in the collision, which is why the first trolley slowed down
Each trolley keeps the momentum it began with, since momentum is a conserved quantity
The momentum lost by the first trolley equals the momentum gained by the second, so the total is unchanged
The second trolley gains momentum but the first loses more, so the total falls in the collision

items.why: In a closed system the total momentum before the event equals the total momentum after it.

items.stem: (physics only) A resultant force acts on an object that is free to move. What does the specification say happens?

options.text: The object's momentum is transferred into the force, which is why the object slows down again
The mass of the object changes, since momentum is mass × velocity and the momentum changes
The object's velocity changes but its momentum does not, because its mass is unchanged
A change in momentum occurs, because the force changes the object's velocity in that time

items.why: 4.5.7.3 states that when a force acts on an object that is moving, or able to move, a change in momentum occurs.

items.stem: (physics only) Which statement describes the equation F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) correctly?

options.text: The force equals the change in momentum, m ∆ v, multiplied by the time over which it changes
The force equals the change in momentum, m ∆ v, divided by the time taken for that change
The force equals the time taken divided by the change in momentum that occurs during it
The force is simply the change in momentum, m ∆ v, whatever the time it takes

items.why: m ∆ v is the change in momentum, so the equation says force equals the rate of change of momentum.

items.stem: (physics only) The specification says force equals the rate of change of momentum. What does 'rate of' add?

options.text: Nothing of substance; the force is simply equal to the change in momentum that takes place
That the momentum is multiplied by the time for which the resultant force acts on the object
That the change in momentum is divided by the time taken for that change to happen
That the momentum changes at a steady rate whenever any resultant force acts on an object

items.why: 'Rate of' means per second, which is why ∆t appears on the bottom of F = (m ∆v)/(∆t).

items.stem: (physics only) Why does an air bag reduce the force on a passenger during a crash?

options.text: It reduces the passenger's change in momentum, so there is less momentum to be got rid of
It absorbs most of the force of the crash, so that only a little of it reaches the passenger
It brings the passenger to rest more quickly, before they can strike anything solid nearby
It increases the time taken for the change in momentum, lowering the rate of change

items.why: The same change in momentum spread over a longer time gives a smaller force, from F = (m ∆v)/(∆t).

items.stem: (physics only) A gymnast lands on a crash mat rather than on the bare floor. Why is the force on the gymnast smaller?

options.text: The mat soaks up much of the force of the landing, so that only a small share of it reaches the gymnast
The mat reduces the gymnast's momentum before the landing, so there is less momentum to be removed
The mat lowers the gymnast's mass on impact, so the change in momentum m ∆ v is made smaller
The mat squashes, so the momentum falls to zero over a longer time, making F = (m ∆v)/(∆t) less

items.why: The change in momentum is the same either way; the mat increases ∆t, which reduces the force.

items.stem: A ball has a mass of 400 g and travels at 5 m/s. What is its momentum?

options.text: 2 kg m/s
80 kg m/s
0.4 kg m/s
2000 kg m/s

items.stem: A skateboarder of mass 60 kg moves at 4 m/s. What is the skateboarder's momentum?

options.text: 15 kg m/s
0.067 kg m/s
240 kg m/s

items.stem: A 40 000 kg lorry moves at 3 m/s. A 1200 kg car moves at 30 m/s. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The car has the greater momentum, because it is the faster moving of the two vehicles
They have equal momentum, since the lorry's extra mass is cancelled by the car's extra speed
The lorry has the greater momentum: 120 000 kg m/s against only 36 000 kg m/s for the car
The lorry has the greater momentum, because momentum simply depends on a vehicle's mass

items.why: 40 000 × 3 = 120 000 kg m/s and 1200 × 30 = 36 000 kg m/s, so the lorry's momentum is larger.

items.stem: A trolley of mass 5 kg has a momentum of 12 kg m/s. What is its velocity?

options.text: 60 m/s

items.why: Rearranging p = m v gives v = p / m = 12 / 5 = 2.4 m/s.

items.stem: (physics only) A 3 kg trolley moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary 2 kg trolley. They stick together. What is their velocity after the collision?

options.text: 4 m/s
12 kg m/s

items.why: Momentum before = 3 × 4 = 12 kg m/s. Afterwards the moving mass is 5 kg, so v = 12 / 5 = 2.4 m/s.

items.stem: (physics only) A 0.5 kg ball moving at 8 m/s hits a stationary 1.5 kg ball. The first ball stops. What is the velocity of the second ball?

options.text: 8 m/s
12 m/s
4 kg m/s

items.why: Momentum before = 0.5 × 8 = 4 kg m/s. All of it passes to the 1.5 kg ball, so v = 4 / 1.5 = 2.7 m/s.

items.stem: (physics only) A 50 kg skater at rest pushes a 15 kg sledge away at 4 m/s. What is the skater's velocity after the push?

options.text: 4 m/s backwards
1.2 m/s backwards
13.3 m/s backwards
60 kg m/s backwards

items.why: The total momentum stays zero, so 50 × v = 15 × 4 = 60, giving v = 1.2 m/s in the opposite direction.

items.stem: (physics only) A 70 kg passenger moving at 12 m/s is stopped in 0.1 s without an air bag, and in 0.6 s with one. What are the two forces?

options.text: 84 N and 504 N
8400 N and 504 N
840 N and 840 N

items.stem: In which of these situations is work done on the object by the force described?

options.text: A sledge is dragged forwards and slides 5 m over snow
A cleaner pushes hard on a crate that does not move
A waiter carries a tray level across a room
A student holds a bag of books still for a minute

items.why: The pulling force causes a displacement of the sledge along its own line of action, so work is done on the sledge.

items.stem: In the equation work done = force × distance, what is meant by the distance?

options.text: The total length of the path that the object takes
The distance the object moves, in any direction
The distance moved along the line of action of the force
The time for which the force carries on acting

items.why: The specification defines the distance as the distance moved along the line of action of the force.

items.stem: Which row gives the correct units for the quantities in W = F s?

options.text: work in newtons, force in newtons, distance in metres
work in joules, force in newtons, distance in metres
work in watts, force in newtons, distance in metres
work in joules, force in newtons, time in seconds

items.why: Work done, W, in joules, J; force, F, in newtons, N; distance, s, in metres.

items.stem: Which statement correctly defines one joule of work?

options.text: The work done when a force of 1 N acts for a time of 1 s
The force of 1 N needed to move an object through 1 m
The work done when 1 N of energy is given to a body
The work done when a force of 1 N causes a displacement of 1 m

items.why: This is the specification definition: one joule of work is done when a force of one newton causes a displacement of one metre.

items.stem: A crane lifts a steel beam steadily upwards. Which statement best describes what happens as the crane's force does work on the beam?

options.text: Energy is transferred to the beam by the crane's force
New energy is created by the crane and passed to the beam
Energy is used up by the crane, so none reaches it
Force is stored inside the beam as it is lifted

items.why: Doing work is a way of transferring energy; the joules of work done equal the joules transferred to the beam.

items.stem: A crate is pushed at a steady speed across a rough floor. What is the main effect of the work done against the frictional forces on the crate?

options.text: The energy transferred is destroyed by friction
The temperature of the crate rises steadily
The kinetic energy of the crate keeps rising
The friction only slows the crate down

items.why: Work done against the frictional forces acting on an object causes a rise in the temperature of the object.

items.stem: A student rubs their hands together quickly and the hands become warmer. Which statement best explains this?

options.text: The movement energy is used up and lost as heat
Warm air trapped between the hands heats them
Work is done against friction at the hands
New heat energy is made by the rubbing

items.why: Work done against the frictional forces acting on the hands causes a rise in their temperature.

items.stem: A force does 250 J of work on a trailer as the trailer is pulled along a track. What does this tell you?

options.text: 250 J of new energy was created by the pulling
250 J of energy was used up and cannot return
A force of 250 N acted on the trailer as it moved
250 J of energy has been transferred to it

items.why: The work done by a force equals the energy it transfers, so the trailer gained 250 J.

items.stem: A student holds a box of weight 40 N still at chest height for 15 s. How much work does the student's upward force do on the box?

options.text: 0 J

items.why: The box has no displacement, so s = 0 and W = 40 × 0 = 0 J.

items.stem: A force of 25 N pushes a trolley 8 m along the line of action of the force. How much work is done on the trolley?

options.text: 3.125 joules
0.32 joules
33 joules
200 joules

items.why: W = F s = 25 × 8 = 200 J, with the distance measured along the line of action of the force.

items.stem: A crane does 3000 J of work on a load using a force of 250 N. How far does the load move along the line of action of the force?
items.why: Rearranging W = F s gives s = W ÷ F = 3000 ÷ 250 = 12 m.

items.stem: A motor does 6000 N m of work. What is this work done in joules?

options.text: 6 J

items.why: 1 joule = 1 newton-metre, so the number is unchanged: 6000 N m = 6000 J.
